Confiscating the Commons, part 1: The invention of proprietary software

It is worth remembering that, historically, software had always been free. Software described ideas, ways of using computers, algorithms and nobody thought you could "own" something like that. Software could be as volatile as some notes on a sheet of paper or verbal instructions about how to plug wires.

When the young Bill Gates wrote his "letter to hobbyists" in 1976, he was trying to convince people to sell and buy software instead of just sharing them, a position that was not widespread at the time. Even Apple replied in ads to advertise the fact that they were favouring free software that could be shared. Richard Stallman doesn’t even remember reading that Bill Gates letter although he was reading that particular magazine.

Apple changed its stance in 1983, suing Franklin, which was copying Apple software to sell clones of Apple’s computers (which were popular because they were the only computers able to run the independent software Visicalc, the first spreadsheet). Apple lost.

Let me repeat this : in 1983, a vendor was selling computers with Apple software, without paying Apple, and the court judged it was perfectly legal.

But Apple appealed the decision.

And won.

The rest is history.

  • Licenses and the invention of proprietary software (linfo2401.net)

Free Software and Open Source

This was not random. The writing had been on the wall. A nascent software industry heavily wanted to make software "proprietary". One of the only person to perceive that confiscation of users’ freedoms was Richard Stallman, who counterattacked by creating the Free Software movement.

Richard Stallman managed to build a whole counterculture but insisted on being "pure". Any proprietary software was evil in his eyes. He foresaw that if you gave up anything to proprietary software, your freedoms would evaporate. You were as free as the least free software of your toolchain.

But most software hackers had to deal with proprietary software. They also saw potential business opportunities by mixing free and proprietary software. That’s how, nearly 15 years after Stallman’s GNU project inception, Eric Raymond and Bruce Perens formalised the "Open Source Software" concept.

Technically, Open Source and Free Software were the same things. The goal was to appeal to businesses by removing the word "free" and distancing the movement from the non-business-minded Stallman.

What Raymond and Perens envisioned was a huge common of Free and Open Source Software. Those could be used to build small proprietary tools on top of them. Under the free market theory, those proprietary tools would be used only because they were absolutely the best. Also, any popular proprietary software would, of course, be relatively quickly implemented as a free software.

This would force proprietary developers to innovate continuously while the commons would be constantly improved. Purely proprietary solutions, like Microsoft was developing, could not be sustainable in the long term, according to Raymond. Open Source would eventually win.

That was the vision, that was the dream.

And, by some aspect, it was right: Open Source won. Most software in use today are based on the Open Source commons. Without Open Source, there would be no Google, no Apple, no Meta, no Netflix.

Open Source: free labour for businesses

Reluctantly at first, businesses started to jump into the Open Source bandwagon. Microsoft was one of the latest but quickly became the biggest when they discovered that, with Open Source, you could freely pillage the commons without any downsides. You could simply use the work done for free by thousands of volunteers. Sure, it might sometimes be required to put their name in some obscure infobox but, even if you forgot, who would care? But if you did, they would sometimes be proud to work for free for you and listen to your suggestions and do even more unpaid labour.

That’s why Microsoft went as far as buying Github to get a monopoly on Free Software forge.

The only thing you needed to be careful was to avoid "copyleft". Fortunately, it was easy to convince free software hackers that copyleft was a "cancer" and that copylefting your code was hurting your chances to become a dot-com billionaire. And to be sure, MIT became the default license on Github.

  • On Open Source and the Sustainability of the Commons (ploum.net)

The end of our freedoms

The main reason why monopolistic companies were so wary to avoid any copylefted code was that copyleft was assuming strong copyright laws, something they wanted. In the grand scheme of things, copyleft was validating the systemic vision of a world where everything is copyrightable. Best of all: most pundits totally missed the power of copyleft. Die hard freedom fans would defend MIT as the true freedom license. It looks like, besides Stallman, nobody really understood copyleft. And Stallman was awkward, to say the least.

  • We need more of Richard Stallman, not less (ploum.net)

See, for example, how Molly White pokes fun at people who want to open their code but not have it reused "like that". She, like many, totally missed the copyleft part.

  • “Wait, not like that”: Free and open access in the age of generative AI (www.citationneeded.news)

The next step in that plundering is to have LLMs trained on our free software commons so they can generate very similar looking codes which, magically, have no license. The copyrighting of the code which was deemed so important by Bill Gates and Apple is, suddenly, not important anymore. Respecting the laws they defended for 40 years might even "kill their business model".

  • Why open source may not survive the rise of generative AI (www.zdnet.com)

We were told that the copyright would protect our work. It is not true anymore. Marcello Vitali-Rosati told it: don’t call it AI, call it privatisation of the commons.

  • Arrêtons de parler d'Intelligence Artificielle: ce n'est que le nom de la privatisation de l'espace public (blog.sens-public.org)

But this privatisation is not new. There’s even a whole strategy for it that I call "Androidification".

  • Confiscating the Commons, part 2: The Androidification of Open Source (ploum.net)
